summary.title: WebGL + Rust: Basic Water Tutorial
summary.one_liner: You learn how a basic real-time water surface is rendered in WebGL using reflection and refraction framebuffers, du/dv distortion, normal maps and Fresnel blending, with a walkthrough of a Rust/WebAssembly demo.
keywords: how to render water in games
takeaways: Water can be approximated by blending a refraction texture (scene below the water) and a reflection texture (scene mirrored above the water) on a flat quad.
A du/dv map offsets texture sampling each frame to make the water appear to move, and a normal map adds surface detail for specular highlights.
The Fresnel effect mixes reflection and refraction based on viewing angle: viewing from above shows more refraction, from the side more reflection.
WebGL has no gl_ClipDistance, so the tutorial clips fragments against a plane in the fragment shader and discards those on the wrong side.
The demo builds Rust to wasm32 with cargo and wasm-bindgen, and exports Blender scenery via a build script.
summary.summary: The tutorial explains the core ideas of rendering water: render the scene below the surface into a refraction framebuffer, mirror the camera across the water plane to render a reflection framebuffer, then blend both on a quad using du/dv distortion, a normal map, depth-based darkening, Fresnel weighting and a specular highlight. It then walks through the demo's Rust and WebAssembly code, including the build script, the index.html render loop, the water vertex and fragment shaders, the clip-plane discard approach, and the uniform setup in the water tile renderer. It is a reference implementation intended as a starting point for more advanced water techniques.
